 A Theoretical Investigation into the Role of Surface Defects for
 Oxygen Evolution on RuO2
 Colin F. Dickens†,‡ and Jens K. Nørskov*,†,‡
 †
 SUNCAT Center for Interface Science and Catalysis, Department of Chemical Engineering, Stanford University, Shriram Center,
 443 Via Ortega, Stanford, California 94305, United States
 ‡
 SUNCAT Center for Interface Science and Catalysis, SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, 2575 Sand Hill Road, Menlo Park,
 California 94025, United States

 S Supporting Information

 ABSTRACT: The inability of conventional theoretical models to corroborate
 the well-known experimental activity of RuO2 for the oxygen evolution reaction
 Downloaded via UNIV OF TOKYO on January 15, 2026 at 09:19:22 (UTC).

 (OER) has recently been the subject of numerous research eﬀorts. In this study,
 we use density functional theory calculations to investigate the possibility that
 surface defects formed during dissolution are responsible for the OER activity of
 RuO2. It has been well-established experimentally that RuO2 undergoes
 dissolution during OER, yet little is known about the atomic structure or
 catalytic reactivity of the resulting defect sites. Through simulation of point
 defects, steps, and kinks derived from the RuO2 (110) surface, we discover a 0.7
 eV range in the primary descriptor for OER activity, with the most active sites
 outperforming those at the ideal (110) surface by nearly 0.5 eV. We postulate
 that these variations in reactivity are due to diﬀerences in the local electronic
 structure, and we investigate in more detail the electronic structure of two singly
 coordinated sites at the same Ru atom located at a kink. Finally, we investigate
 possible dissolution pathways that may proceed at the RuO2 surface under OER conditions.

far on a theoretical overpotential volcano plot with an assumed can have activities that diﬀer by as much as 0.31 eV. We have
 highlighted one of these cases, namely the CUS-terminated
 single-kink in Figure 6, and we use a density of states analysis to
 examine the variations in local electronic structure that may
 inﬂuence bonding at the RuO2 surface. The energies of the d-
 states that couple to either of the singly bound oxygens can be
 probed by projecting the density of states onto Ru before oxygen
 adsorption. The states contributing to the Ru−O bond pointing
 out of the (110) plane are isolated by projecting onto the dz2
 states of Ru, while the states of the adjacent Ru−O bond can be
 isolated by projecting onto the dx2−y2 states of Ru. Figure 6B
 shows these projections upon removal of both O atoms and a
 single self-consistent DFT calculation. As shown in Figure 6,
 the dx2−y2 states are shifted to signiﬁcantly higher energies
 compared to the dz2 states, and this is reﬂected in a d-band
 center that is more than 0.5 eV higher lying. Within the d-band
 model that has been very successful at describing the reactivity
 of metal surfaces based on their electronic structure,44 we might
 expect these higher-lying d states to result in less ﬁlling of the
 Ru−O antibonding states and thus a stronger Ru−O bond.

molecule, we can use eq 6 to determine the chemical potential
of the assumed dissolution product, RuO4(aq), which is our
reference state for dissolution calculations. Because dissolution
intermediates at the RuO2 surface may bear some resemblance
to the ﬁnal dissolution product, we believe it important to
benchmark our ability to describe RuO4-like species. While it is
not trivial to simulate the dissolved RuO4(aq) in eq 6, we can
approximate it as RuO4(l), which may be reasonable considering
